en: (Vv 216) Homage to the Buddha!
If the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena does not exist anywhere, [then...]
Your statement, being devoid of intrinsic nature, is not capable of negating intrinsic nature.

If it is held that all phenomena are empty because an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not found anywhere— neither in their causes, nor in their conditions, nor in the collection of causes and conditions, nor apart from them— then indeed,
the sprout does not exist within the seed which serves as its cause.
It does not exist in each individual factor designated as a condition—such as earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth;
nor in the conditions collectively; nor in the causal conditions collectively; nor in the totality of the causal conditions; nor apart from the causal conditions altogether.
Since its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not exist therein, the sprout is therefore devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
Because it is without intrinsic nature, it is empty.
Just as this sprout is without intrinsic nature and is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature, so too all things are empty because they lack intrinsic nature. (Vv 218)
To this we reply:
if it is so for you as well, then even that statement of yours—"all things are empty"—is itself empty. What is the reason? Because that too does not exist in its cause.
It does not exist within the primary elements, whether associated or dissociated,

nor among the conditions such as the chest, throat, lips, tongue, roots of the teeth, palate, nose, head, and so forth; it does not exist even in the totality of both, nor does it exist separately, entirely apart from the collection of causes and conditions.
Since it does not exist anywhere here,
it is therefore without intrinsic nature;
since it is without intrinsic nature, [it is empty].
Therefore it is empty;
therefore, it is impossible for this [emptiness] to effect the negation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
What is the reason?
For that which is non-existent cannot be burned by fire,
nor can it be cut by a non-existent weapon,

nor can it be moistened by non-existent waters; likewise, by means of a non-existent statement, the negation of the intrinsic nature of all things can be effected, but the intrinsic nature of all things cannot be made to cease.
In this regard, as for what was stated—that the intrinsic nature of all things is negated, and thus the intrinsic nature of things is excluded everywhere—that is not so.
(Vv 220) Now,
if this statement possesses intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), your previous thesis is destroyed;
there would be an inconsistency, and you must state the specific reason for that distinction.
Furthermore, if you think that this fault must not arise, [you might argue that] this statement possesses an intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*),

and because it possesses an intrinsic nature, it is not empty (*aśūnya*). Therefore, by this [statement], the intrinsic nature of all things is negated, and the intrinsic nature of all things is turned back.
To this we reply:
your proposition that all intrinsic natures are empty is itself destroyed.
Furthermore, that statement of yours is included within all things.
Why? Because your statement is non-empty among all things; since it is non-empty, the intrinsic nature of all things has been negated by it.
Thus, a discourse involving six alternatives (ṣaṭkoṭika) follows. How so? Well then, if all things are empty, your statement is also empty, because your statement is included among all things.
Because that [negation] is empty, a negation is untenable.

In that case, the negation that "all things are empty" is untenable. (1) If, on the other hand, the negation "all things are empty" were tenable, then because your own statement is empty, this negation would be untenable. (2)
Now, if all things are empty while your statement is not empty, then by that [statement] which performs the negation, your statement is not included in "everything.
In that case, there is a contradiction with the example.
Furthermore, if your statement is indeed included in "everything" and all things are empty, [then your statement itself must be empty].
Therefore, that [negation] is also empty because of its emptiness; thus, there is no negation by this [emptiness].

(4) Alternatively, if emptiness exists and by it there is the negation that "all things are empty," then all things, though empty, would either be capable of performing functions or incapable of them.
And this is not desired. (5)

Now, [the opponent argues]: "If all things (*sarvabhāva*) are empty, they cannot be capable of performing an action (*kriyā*), lest there be a contradiction with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*). Therefore, the negation of the intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) of all things by your empty statement is not tenable. (6) Furthermore: "In this way, because that [statement] exists, the consequence of inequality (*vaiṣamikatvaprasaṅga*) follows."
"Something is empty and something is non-empty.
Regarding this inequality, a specific reason must be stated—
that specific reason by which something would be empty and something else non-empty.
And since that reason has not been taught,
the statement that "all things are empty" is not tenable.
Furthermore,
another point: if it occurs to you that [the self] is like sound, this is not tenable.
In this case, there is a prevention of that which is yet to come by means of a sound that exists [at present].
It might occur to you that it is just as if someone were to say, "Do not make a sound,
do not make a sound," and by that very sound, a cessation is brought about;
in the same way, [it is said that] all things are empty.
"By means of an empty statement, the exclusion of the intrinsic nature of all things is effected in every respect.
To this we say:
even this is untenable; for what reason?
For in this case, by means of an existent word, the negation of a future word is performed;
however, here, by your statement, the negation of the intrinsic nature of all things is not being performed. For according to your own view, even the statement itself is non-existent.
The intrinsic nature of all things is also non-existent;
therefore, this presentation of the object—"let it not be like sound"—is [itself] non-existent.
Furthermore,
if it were thought that even the object to be negated is likewise [non-existent], that too would be simply non-existent.
Thus, your proposition is refuted by its own definition, not mine.
It may occur to you that the negation, as well as the object to be negated, is untenable according to this very same reasoning;
therefore, that which you negate— the indication of the negation of the intrinsic nature of all things—
is itself untenable.
To this we reply:
this very thing is indeed existent by virtue of its sound.
Why? Because you, and not I, state here that this has attained the characteristics of a thesis (*pratijñā*).
"I do not say that all things are empty;
therefore, I do not withdraw from your proposition. The previous position is not mine."
In that regard, as for what was said— "the negation and the object to be negated are likewise considered [to exist]"—
that is untenable.
Furthermore:
If you were to negate entities after having perceived them through direct perception,
that direct perception by which entities are perceived does not exist.
If you claim that all things are empty based on perceiving all things through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that is untenable.
Why? Because even direct perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is empty, since it is included within intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Even he who perceives all entities is himself empty; therefore, by means of direct perception as a valid cognition, there is no entity that is perceived, and the negation of what is not perceived is untenable. [The claim] that "all entities are empty" is thus unestablished.
It might occur to you that,
having apprehended all things through inference, scripture, or presumption, the exclusion of all things is thereby effected.
To this we reply:

inference, as well as scripture and analogy, have already been refuted by means of perception; for those objects that are established through inference, scripture, or examples [are likewise refuted]. (NagVv 6)
Inference, as well as comparison and verbal testimony, have been refuted by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For just as the means of valid cognition that is direct perception is empty because all things are empty,
so too are inference, comparison, and verbal testimony empty.

Because all entities (*bhāva*) are empty, even those objects established by inference, those established by scripture (*āgama*), and those established by analogy (*upamāna*) are also empty, because all entities are empty. Furthermore, whoever perceives entities by means of inference, analogy, and scripture is also empty. Therefore, there is no perception of entities; for those that are not perceived—
Furthermore, the negation of intrinsic nature is untenable.
Therefore, that which was stated—that all phenomena are empty—is not correct.
Furthermore,
those who know the states of phenomena consider [this] to be the state of wholesome phenomena.
This application [of the argument] regarding the nature of things is also valid for the remaining [categories], such as the wholesome.
In this regard, those who know the states of phenomena consider that there are one hundred and nineteen wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*),
namely: a portion of consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

Of contact, mental attention, aspiration, resolve, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, equanimity, application, conjunction, attainment, resolute intention, abstention, determination, zeal, upward-striving, enthusiasm,
indefatigability, mastery, practice, freedom from regret, steadfastness, and perseverance.
of the failure to see, of the lack of inference, of the lack of penetration;
of the attainment [of worldly goals], of the vow, of intoxication, of separation from sense objects,
and of the destruction of the state of non-emancipation.
Of stability, of impermanence, of that which has reached its full capacity, of aging, of exhaustion, of weariness, of discursive thoughts, of joy, of negligence, of lack of tranquility,
and of conventional discourse.
Of looking [at one] with aversion or with favor; of confidence or reverence; of wonder or devotion; of lack of devotion or service; of respect or disrespect;
of relaxation; of laughter or speech; of trembling or success; of lack of clarity or lack of relaxation; and of worldly conduct.
Of skillfulness, gentleness, remorse,
and sorrow; of exertion, freedom from weariness, lack of perverse grasping, accumulation, the purities of the vows, the resolute intention, and form.

Faith, modesty, straightforwardness, honesty, tranquility, stainlessness, clarity, gentleness, discernment, disenchantment, freedom from feverish distress, absence of intoxication, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, non-attachment, non-abandonment, mastery over existence, lack of trepidation, lack of hypocrisy, honor, compassion, loving-kindness, and lack of dejection.
Absence of resentment, absence of malice, and the thorough pervading of the mind with patience—
this is the portion consisting of perseverance and serenity;
it is merit.
The attainment of non-perception,
the state of leading to liberation, omniscience, and unconditioned phenomena— these constitute one hundred and nineteen wholesome factors, which are the wholesome intrinsic nature.
Likewise, for unwholesome [phenomena], the unwholesome is their intrinsic nature;
[the nature of] obscured-unspecified [phenomena] is [obscured-unspecified].
For those that are innate and indeterminate, [the retribution] is innate and indeterminate;
for those spoken of as belonging to the desire realm, it belongs to the desire realm;
for those spoken of as belonging to the form realm, it belongs to the form realm.
For those taught as formless, it is that which is taught as formless;
for those that are untainted, it is the untainted;
for those taught as suffering, it is that which is taught as suffering.
He is the speaker on origination for those things spoken of as origination; the speaker on cessation for those things spoken of as cessation;
and the speaker on the path for those things spoken of as the path.
That which is to be abandoned by cultivation is [the result] of those things to be abandoned by cultivation; that which is not to be abandoned is [the result] of those things not to be abandoned;
and that which is to be abandoned is [the result] of those things to be abandoned.

Since the intrinsic nature of phenomena is thus seen to be of many kinds, therefore that which was stated here— that "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature, and because they lack intrinsic nature they are empty"— is not tenable.
Furthermore:
that which is the nature of the dharma leading to liberation, and those things which lead to liberation— of these...
And [the same applies] to those very states of phenomena that have been described as leading to liberation and so forth.

And here, for those factors that lead to deliverance which have been described according to their respective states, dharma is the nature of leading to deliverance; for those that do not lead to deliverance, it is the nature of not leading to deliverance;
and for those that constitute the limbs of enlightenment, it is the nature of being limbs of enlightenment.

Among those that are not factors of enlightenment, he is one who is not a factor of enlightenment; among those that are factors conducive to enlightenment, he is one who is a factor conducive to enlightenment;
among those that are not factors conducive to enlightenment, he is one who is not a factor conducive to enlightenment.
Thus it is for the remaining [categories] as well; for this reason, since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena is seen to be of many kinds,
that which was stated— that "all things are without intrinsic nature" and "because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty"— is not [the case].
Furthermore:

If there were no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena such that they are "without intrinsic nature," then even the name [“without intrinsic nature”] would not exist; for a name cannot exist without a referent.
And if the intrinsic nature of phenomena were non-empty because of the existence of the intrinsic natures of things, then all things would be non-empty;
in that case, what was stated—that all things are empty because they lack intrinsic nature—would not be true.
Furthermore:
If intrinsic nature exists, yet it is not found in phenomena, therefore—
It is appropriate to teach that which possesses an intrinsic nature apart from phenomena.
Now, if you think that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists so that a name might not be without a basis,
yet that [intrinsic nature] does not exist in phenomena (dharmas),
then in this way the emptiness of phenomena will be established because of the lack of intrinsic nature in phenomena.
"And yet, a name cannot be without a referent.
To this we reply:
"In that case, to what would that intrinsic nature now belong? It is logical to teach that the referent is something distinct from the dharma."
And since that has not been taught, the conceptualization that there is an intrinsic nature of phenomena is inferior.
Furthermore:
Since this negation— "there is no jar in the house"—
is observed to be a negation of that which exists, therefore, for you, there is a negation of an existing intrinsic nature.
And here, a negation is made of an object that exists in name only;
for example, "there is no jar in the house.
What is negated is the jar that [merely] exists.
Not of that which is non-existent.

In this very way, when it is said that "there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena," this results in the negation of an intrinsic nature that actually exists, rather than one that does not exist.
In this regard, as for what was said—
that all things are empty because they lack intrinsic nature— that is not so.
For it is precisely because negation is possible that the intrinsic nature of all things is not negated.
(Vv 242) Now, if that intrinsic nature does not exist, why is it not negated by you through this speech? For the negation of a non-existent thing is established even without speech.
By this statement, "there is no intrinsic nature at all," what is being negated by you when you say that "entities are without intrinsic nature"?
For the negation of what is non-existent is established even without words,
just as, for example, the coldness of fire.
This is the nature of stability.
Furthermore:
it is like the false perception of water in a mirage by the ignorant.
In this way, there would be a false apprehension on your part; for that which is non-existent is indeed being negated.

It may occur to you that just as children have the grasping of false water in a mirage, so too a person of wise nature says, "That mirage is indeed devoid of water," in order to turn back that false grasping; likewise,
in order to turn back the grasping at intrinsic nature by sentient beings regarding things that are without intrinsic nature, it is said that "all things are without intrinsic nature."
Thus it is said.
To this we reply:
If that were so, would there not then exist the grasping, the object to be grasped, and the grasper?
The negation, the object of negation, and the negation itself—this constitutes a group of six.

If this is so, then indeed, while this is the case, there exists the false grasping of sentient beings; there exists the object of grasp, there exist sentient beings who are the graspers, and there exists the negation; for that false grasping as well, there exists that which is to be negated, namely, what is called the "object of false grasping."
There are refuters of this false grasping, such as yourselves; thus, the hexad is established.
Because this hexad is well-established, that which was said—that all things are empty—is not so.
Now, if there is neither grasping, nor that which is grasped, nor graspers; then neither negation, nor that which is negated, nor those who negate exist either.
Now, thinking "let this fault not occur," one might hold that there is neither grasping, nor anything to be grasped, nor a grasper.
This being the case, even that negation of grasping—namely, that "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature"—does not exist;
for there is neither an object to be negated, nor are there any negators.
If the negation, the object to be negated, and the agent of negation do not exist,
then all things are established, whose intrinsic nature is thus.
And if there is neither negation, nor the object of negation, nor negators, then all things are unnegated, and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all things exists.
Furthermore:

Since there is no establishment of a reason from itself due to its lack of intrinsic nature, how indeed could you have a reason? And the establishment of this matter of yours, being without a reason, is not tenable.
Regarding the point that "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature," your reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.

Why? Because since all things are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are empty; therefore, no reason can be derived from them. In the absence of a reason, how could the thesis "all things are empty"—which would thus be without a reason—ever be established?
In that regard, as for what was said—that all things are empty—that is not so.
Furthermore:
If, for you, the establishment of the negation of intrinsic nature occurs without a cause, then for me as well, the existence of intrinsic nature is established without a cause. (NagVv 18)
Now, if you think that the establishment of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of entities is causeless—
just as for you the production of intrinsic nature is established as being causeless—
then for me as well, the existence of intrinsic nature is likewise established as being causeless.
(Vv 248) Now,
if the existence of a cause implies that things lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*), this is untenable;
for in the world, because of the absence of intrinsic nature, not a single thing exists as a real entity.
In this case, if you maintain that the reason exists,
then the claim that "all things are devoid of intrinsic nature" is untenable.
What is the reason?
For indeed, in the world, there is no entity whatsoever that is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore:
If the negation comes first and the object to be negated afterwards, that is not tenable;
nor is it tenable if they are simultaneous, because [in either case] the intrinsic nature would be non-existent. (NagVv 20)
In this case, if the negation occurs first and the object of negation afterwards,
then the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvya) is not established; for if the object of negation does not exist, of what would there be a negation?
Furthermore, it is not tenable for the negation to be posterior and the object of negation to be prior;
for if the object of negation is already established, what does the negation accomplish?

Or if the negation and the object of negation are simultaneous, even then, the object of negation is not the cause of the fact of being negated, nor is there a negation of that which is to be negated.
Nor is there [causality] in the case of a negation;
for example, in the case of two horns produced simultaneously, the right horn is not the cause of the left, nor is the left the cause of the right.
Therefore, that which was stated—that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature—is not [correct].
To this it is replied: As for what was stated by you— that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all things does not exist anywhere— [we respond as follows].
"Your statement, being devoid of intrinsic nature (asvabhāva), is not capable of negating intrinsic nature.
To this we reply:
"If my word does not exist even when separated from the collection of causes and conditions," [then it cannot negate yours].
Is it not the case that the emptiness of entities is established because they lack intrinsic nature?

If my words do not exist in the primary elements (mahābhūtas), nor in the associated (saṃprayukta) or dissociated (viprayukta) conditions, nor in the collection [of factors] such as the chest, throat, tongue, teeth, palate, nose, head, and so forth; and if they do not exist apart from this collection of causes and conditions, then they are without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty (śūnya).
Thus,
is it not established that this speech of mine is empty because it lacks intrinsic nature?
And just as this speech of mine is empty due to its lack of intrinsic nature, [so too is everything else].
Likewise, all things are empty because they lack intrinsic nature;
therefore, your statement that "because your own words are empty, the emptiness of all things is not tenable" is incorrect.
(Vv 252) Furthermore:
And he who says that the emptiness of phenomena depends [on them]— [refute] him.
For that which exists dependently indeed lacks intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, because you do not understand the meaning of the emptiness of entities, you state this critique regarding their arising; yet, since your own words are empty and your words lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is logically untenable to negate the intrinsic nature of entities by means of such words that themselves lack intrinsic nature.
For here, that which is the existence of things through dependence is emptiness.
Why? Because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
For those things which have arisen dependently do not possess an intrinsic nature.
Because of the absence of intrinsic nature;
therefore, because they depend upon causes and conditions.
For if things were to exist by way of their own intrinsic nature, [they would not depend on causes and conditions].
Even if they were to exist apart from causes and conditions, they do not so exist.
Therefore, they are without intrinsic nature; and because they lack intrinsic nature, they are designated as "empty."

In the same way, my own statement is also dependently originated; because it is dependently originated, it lacks intrinsic nature, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty—this is logically established. (Vv 254)

And just as things such as chariots, cloth, and jars— being dependently originated— are empty of intrinsic nature, yet they function in their respective purposes, such as carrying wood, carrying water, holding honey, water, or milk, and providing protection against cold, wind, and heat; so too this speech of mine, being dependently originated, is devoid of intrinsic nature, and it functions to establish the absence of intrinsic nature in all conditioned phenomena.

As for what was said— that because your statement lacks intrinsic nature it is empty, and because it is empty, the negation of the intrinsic nature of all things by means of it is established— that is not correct.
Furthermore:
An emanation [created] by an emanation, or a man of illusion created by his own magic.
Just as [the negation] negates, so too would that which is being negated be exactly like it.
Just as one might prevent a person created by magic who is engaged in some purpose from acting,
or as a phantom man produced by a magician might prevent another phantom man from acting— yet neither would prevent the other from engaging in any purpose whatsoever;
in that case, the person created by magic who is prevented is empty, and the one who prevents him is likewise an empty phantom man— even so, by my own words which are empty, all things [are negated].
The negation of intrinsic nature is established.

In this regard, as for what you have stated—that because your own words are empty, the negation of the intrinsic nature of all things is not tenable—that is not so. The "sixfold discourse" (*ṣaṭkoṭiko vāda*) has been explained, and it is precisely that which is thus refuted. For this being the case, my word is neither included among all things, nor is it non-empty, nor are all things non-empty.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"If this statement possesses intrinsic nature, then your previous proposition is destroyed."
Regarding the point that "there would be inconsistency in that case and a specific reason must be stated," we say this in response:
this statement is not based on an inherent nature; therefore, there is no loss of my position.
There is no partiality, nor can a specific reason [for such partiality] be stated.
To begin with, this statement of mine is not endowed with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), as was stated previously.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
And since this statement of mine is empty, and all other phenomena (*bhāva*) are also empty, there is no inconsistency.
For if we were to say,
"This statement is non-empty, while all remaining entities are empty," then there would indeed be an inconsistency;
but since this is not the case, there is no inconsistency.
Since it is impossible for there to be an inconsistency— namely, that this statement is non-empty while all other things are empty—
therefore we need not state a specific reason why this statement is non-empty while all things are empty.
Consequently, what you said— that you have lost your argument, that there is an inconsistency, and that you must provide a specific reason— is incorrect.
Furthermore, as for what you have stated—
"Let not [the reason] be like sound"— this does not occur to your mind, nor is this logically tenable.
"For here, by means of a sound that exists, there is the warding off of one that will exist.
To this we reply:
"Let it not be like sound"—this example which you have brought forward against me is not valid.
For that [negation] is indeed by means of a word; and this very [negation] is not the negation of the word itself.
Nor is this an illustration for us:
just as someone who says, "Do not make a sound," while actually making a sound, thereby negates sound;
in the same way, [you] negate emptiness by means of an empty statement.
What is the reason?
For in this example, the exclusion of sound by means of sound is effected;
yet we do not assert that this is the case here.
"All things are without intrinsic nature because they lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they are not non-empty.
What is the reason for this?
If indeed there were a negation of the absence of intrinsic nature by means of the absence of intrinsic nature,
then upon the cessation of the absence of intrinsic nature, intrinsic nature itself would be established.
Just as the exclusion of sound is effected by the word "do not make a sound," so too,
if the exclusion of things that lack intrinsic nature were effected by a statement that itself lacks intrinsic nature, then this analogy would be applicable.
However, in this case, the negation of the intrinsic nature of entities is effected by a statement that lacks intrinsic nature.

Thus, if by means of a statement that is itself devoid of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvyena vacanena*) the negation of the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvyapratiṣedha*) were made for things that lack intrinsic nature, then precisely because of that negation of the lack of intrinsic nature, those things would possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*);
and because they possess intrinsic nature, they would be non-empty (*aśūnya*).
"We declare that things are empty, not non-empty; therefore, this [objection] is without any supporting example.
Alternatively, it is like the false grasping at a woman in a magically created woman, thinking, "This is a woman."
If a created being were to strike someone, one might think: "This much [is real]. // NagVv_27 //

Alternatively, suppose some person were to have a false attachment, thinking "this is a woman," toward a magically created woman who is empty of intrinsic nature from the perspective of ultimate reality;
he might indeed give rise to passion for her because of that false attachment.
It would be just as if a magical creation had been produced by a Tathāgata or by one of his disciples.
By the empowerment of a Tathāgata or by the empowerment of a disciple of a Tathāgata, one would turn back that false grasping.

In the same way, by means of empty words resembling a magical creation (*nirmitaka*), this grasping at intrinsic nature—which occurs toward things that are like magically created women and are devoid of self-nature—is turned back and refuted.
Therefore, this example is applicable for establishing emptiness, and no other is.
Alternatively, this reason is "identical to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*), for there is no existence of sound [apart from its conventional reality];
moreover, we do not speak without relying upon worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*). (NagVv 28)
The reason "like sound" is merely equivalent to the probandum (sādhyasama).
Why? Because all entities are indistinguishable in their lack of intrinsic nature (naiḥsvabhāvya);
for that sound, too, is dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna).
The existence of intrinsic nature does not exist,
because that existence of intrinsic nature is non-existent;
as it has been said:
For here, by means of the word, there would be a negation of that which is to exist;
thus, that [position] is contradicted.
Moreover, we do not speak while rejecting conventional truth or without accepting conventional truth.
"All phenomena are empty.
For it is not possible to perform the teaching of the Dharma without relying upon conventional truth,
as it has been said:
"Without relying upon conventional usage, the ultimate truth is not taught;
without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvāṇa is not realized.
[MMK 24.18] Therefore, just like my own words, all things are empty, and the absence of intrinsic nature in all things is established in both ways.
Furthermore, as for what you have stated—
that it might be thought that "the negation and the object of negation are likewise"— that is simply not so.
"In this way, your proposition would be refuted by its own definition, but mine would not.
To this we reply:
"If there were any proposition at all in that regard, then that would be my fault."
And since I have no thesis, there is no fault on my part whatsoever.

If I had any thesis (*pratijñā*), then, because I would have fallen under the definition of a thesis, that aforementioned fault would apply. However, as you have stated regarding entities (*bhāva*), so it would be for me; yet I have no thesis whatsoever. Therefore, since all entities are empty, utterly stilled, and by nature secluded, how could there be the attainment of the definition of a thesis? And how could there be a fault arising from the attainment of the definition of a thesis?
In that regard, as for what you stated— that the fault belongs to you alone because [the argument] falls under the definition of a proposition— that is not so.
Furthermore, as for what you stated:
If you first negate entities by apprehending them through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then that direct perception by which those entities are apprehended does not exist.
Inference (*anumāna*) has already been refuted by [the critique of] direct perception; the same applies to scripture (*āgama*) and analogy (*upamāna*).
And those objects which are to be established by inference and scripture, as well as those to be established by examples— regarding these,
we say:
if I were to perceive anything at all, I would either engage with it or withdraw from it.
Since that [object] does not exist through means such as direct perception, I am beyond reproach.

If I were to perceive any object whatsoever by means of direct perception, inference, [comparison, or verbal testimony]— by these reasons and instruments of knowledge, or by any one of the four instruments of knowledge— then...
Therefore, since I do not perceive even the slightest object to be engaged with, I neither engage nor desist. This being the case, the two objections you have raised— namely,
that "if you were to negate entities after perceiving them by means of one or another of the instruments of knowledge such as direct perception"— do not apply.

"But surely the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been stated by you, and the objects to be known are also established by those very means of valid cognition; thus, this objection of mine remains entirely valid.
[Response:
If the establishment of each of those various objects were indeed through the means of valid cognition...
Furthermore, tell me how those means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are established.
If you consider that the establishment of those various objects of cognition is by means of valid cognition— just as the objects of measurement are established by the instruments of measurement—
then from what source is the establishment of these four means of valid cognition themselves: namely, perception, inference, comparison, and scripture?

If, first of all, there were a means of valid cognition for those things that lack a means of valid cognition, then there would be no establishment of a beginning, nor of a middle, nor of an end. Furthermore, if you think that the establishment of objects occurs through means of valid cognition— that is, the establishment of objects is by means of valid cognitions—
then your thesis is abandoned.
(Vv 274) Nevertheless,
if the establishment of a means of valid cognition were to occur through other means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress.
In that case, there is no establishment of a beginning, nor indeed of a middle, nor of an end.

If, however, you think that the establishment of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that the establishment of those means of valid cognition occurs through other means of valid cognition, there follows the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
What is the fault in the consequence of infinite regress?
There is no establishment of a beginning there, nor indeed of a middle, nor of an end.
In this case, due to the consequence of infinite regress, there is no establishment of a beginning.
Why? Because those very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would require establishment by other means of valid cognition, and those others by yet others; thus, there is no beginning.
Since there is no beginning, how could there be a middle, and how could there be an end?
Therefore, it is not tenable that those means of valid cognition are established by other means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, if their establishment occurs without means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the [opponent's] argument is abandoned;
moreover, in that case, an inconsistency would arise, and a specific reason for it must be stated.

Now, if you think that those means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are established without [further] means of valid cognition, whereas the objects of cognition (prameyas), which are entities, are established by means of valid cognition— if this were so, your thesis that "objects are established by means of valid cognition" would be abandoned, and there would be an inconsistency regarding some things.
Furthermore, one must state the specific reason why some objects are established by means of valid cognitions while others are not—
the reason by which certain objects are established through valid cognitions and others are not.
Since that [reason] has not been taught, this conception as well is untenable.
Here it is said: "The means of valid cognition themselves establish both their own nature and the nature of others. As it has been stated:
'Just as fire illuminates itself, so too does it illuminate others;
thus the means of valid cognition establish both their own nature and that of others.'"
Namely, one's own self as if it were another, and the self of another as if it were one's own.
To this it is said:
This is an unequal comparison; for fire does not illuminate itself.
For its non-perception is not observed, unlike that of a jar in the darkness.
This comparison is indeed flawed. It is not the case that means of valid cognition establish both themselves and other objects in the same way as fire;
for fire does not illuminate itself.

For if, just as previously a jar in the dark is not perceived because it has not been illuminated by fire, but is perceived at a later time once it has been illuminated by fire—exactly so, if fire were not illuminated by itself beforehand, there would be illumination of the fire at a later time. Therefore, it would have to illuminate its own self; but this is not the case.
Therefore, this conception also is not tenable.
Furthermore: (Vv 280) what else?
And if this fire illuminates itself by means of your statement,
then the consumer of oblations would not burn itself, just as it does not burn another.
And if, according to your statement, fire illuminates its own self just as it illuminates another object,
then surely it would also burn its own self just as it burns another object.
But this is not so;
therefore, that which was stated—that fire illuminates itself just as it illuminates another—is incorrect.
Furthermore:
If fire illuminates both itself and others according to your statement,
then darkness will likewise conceal both itself and others, just like the sacrificial fire.
And if, according to your view, fire illuminates both its own self and the selves of others,
then surely darkness, which is its opposite, would also conceal both its own self and the selves of others;
yet this is not accepted.
In this regard, that which was stated—that fire illuminates both itself and other things—is not correct.
Furthermore:
There is no darkness in fire, nor is there darkness where fire resides within another entity.
How can that which is illumination perform illumination? For illumination is indeed the destruction of darkness.
In this fire there is no darkness,
nor is there darkness where the fire is;
and since illumination is defined as the obstruction of darkness, how could this darkness exist therein?
Fire produces resistance;
through this resistance, it illuminates both itself and other things.
He said: Since it is thus that there is no darkness in fire,
nor is there darkness where fire is,
for this reason fire does not illuminate either itself or others.
For indeed, by that very fire as it is arising, how could there be an obstruction of darkness? Therefore, there is no darkness in the fire, nor is there darkness where the fire is.
Because the fire, at the very moment of its arising, illuminates both itself and other things.
To this it is said:
the claim that fire illuminates only while it is in the very process of arising is an untenable doctrine.
For fire, even as it is arising, does not reach the darkness.
"This fire, at the very moment of its arising, illuminates both itself and others"—this statement is not tenable.
Why? Because fire, at the very moment of its arising, does not come into contact with darkness.
Because it has not reached [the object], it does not destroy it;
and because darkness is not destroyed, there is no illumination.
Alternatively, if fire were to destroy darkness even without having reached it, [it would follow that it destroys everything].
This darkness situated here would destroy [all things] in all world-systems.

Furthermore, if you think that fire destroys darkness even without reaching it, then surely fire situated here would destroy the darkness residing in all world-systems, since it is equally unattained; yet this is not observed. Therefore, the claim that fire destroys darkness without reaching it is incorrect.
(Vv 286) And if, for you, the establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs by itself without depending on the objects of cognition,
then the establishment of the means of valid cognition exists [independently], for establishment does not depend on anything else.
And if you think that the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic, like fire,
then why would their establishment not occur even without depending upon the objects of cognition (*prameya*)?
For that which is intrinsic does not depend upon another.
Now, it might be argued that there is no establishment [of the means of knowledge] through themselves.
To this he says: "If the means of knowledge do not depend upon the objects to be known, what fault will there be? To this it is replied:
"If their establishment as means of knowledge were independent of the objects to be known..."
These means of valid cognition do not exist for anyone in such a manner.
If the establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs without depending on the objects to be cognized,
then these very means of valid cognition would not be means of valid cognition for anyone;
such is the fault.
Now, if for someone there are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
they do not at all become means of valid cognition without depending upon the objects to be cognized (*prameya*).

(Vv 288) Now, if it is thought that their establishment is dependent [on something else], what fault is there in this? For that which is already established requires no proof; indeed, that which is not yet established does not depend on another. (NagVv 42)
Furthermore, if it is thought that the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs in dependence upon the objects to be cognized (*prameya*),
then, this being the case, you are establishing the fourfold set of means of valid cognition as something already established.
What is the reason for this?
For there can be no dependence upon an object that is unestablished;

indeed, an unestablished Devadatta does not depend on any object whatsoever, nor is the establishment of what is already established desired, because a cause for what has already been produced is untenable.
Furthermore:

If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established in every way in dependence upon the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then the establishment of the objects of cognition would occur without depending on the means of valid cognition at all. (NagVv 43)

If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established in dependence upon the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then the objects of cognition are not now established in dependence upon the means of valid cognition. Why? Because that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) does not establish the means of proof (*sādhana*), nor does the means of proof establish itself.
And the means of accomplishment (sādhana) are,
it is said, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the objects of cognition (prameya).
(Vv 290) Furthermore:
if the establishment of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) occurs entirely independently of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [then what need is there for them?]
What is the use of establishing means of valid cognition for those things which are already established by whatever means they are established?
And if you think that the establishment of objects of cognition occurs without depending at all on the means of valid cognition,
then what is the purpose of your inquiry into the establishment of those means of valid cognition?
For what end indeed would those means of valid cognition be investigated?
If those objects of cognition were established without means of cognition, what would be the use of means of cognition there?
But if the establishment of the means of cognition occurs only by depending upon those objects of cognition,
then in that case, the relationship between the means of cognition and the objects of cognition is certainly reversed.

Moreover, if you think that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist only by depending upon the objects of cognition (*prameya*), thinking thus so that the aforementioned fault may not occur— then, this being the case for you, there would be a reversal of the order of the means of valid cognition.
Your means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) become objects of valid cognition (prameya),
because they are established by objects of valid cognition;
and the means of valid cognition also become objects of valid cognition.
Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the establishers [of their objects].

Now, for you, the establishment of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) depends upon the establishment of the means of valid cognition, and the establishment of the means of valid cognition depends upon the establishment of the objects of cognition.
The establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs; for you, however, there is no establishment of either one.
Now, if you think that the establishment of the object of cognition occurs through the establishment of the means of cognition because it depends upon the means of cognition,
and that the establishment of the means of cognition occurs through the establishment of the object of cognition because it depends upon the object of cognition;
This being so, there is no establishment of either [of the two].
For if the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are established by means of the instruments of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how will those very instruments,
which are themselves yet to be established by those same objects of cognition, establish them?
For if objects of cognition are established by means of valid cognitions, then those very valid cognitions must be established by those same objects of cognition.
But surely, since the objects of cognition are unestablished, the cause [of their establishment] is itself unestablished; being unestablished, how will they establish the objects of cognition?
If the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are established by the objects of cognition (prameyas),
and those [objects] are themselves to be established by those very [means], how will they establish them?

If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established by the objects of cognition (*prameya*), and those objects of cognition must in turn be established by those very same means of valid cognition—

well then, since the means of valid cognition are unestablished, how will the means of valid cognition establish [the objects], given that their cause is unestablished? It would be like a son who is to be produced by a father, yet who must produce that very father by means of that son.
If that father is something to be produced, tell me: who produces whom there?
It is just as if someone were to say:
"A son is to be produced by a father, and that father is to be produced by the son.
Now, tell me: by whom is whom to be produced?
In exactly that same way, you indeed say:

"The objects of cognition are to be established by means of the instruments of cognition, and yet those very instruments of cognition are [established] by those objects of cognition. In that case, now, which ones are to be established by which?
Who is the father and who is the son? Tell us that, and how both of them possess the characteristics of both father and son, for we have a doubt in this matter.

Regarding those two previously mentioned, the father and the son, tell us: which is the son and which is the father? For both of them possess the characteristics of a father because they are procreators, and they possess the characteristics of a son because they are produced; thus, we have a doubt here as to which among them is the father and which is the son.
In the same way, regarding these which exist— the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition—
among them, which are the means of valid cognition and which are the objects of valid cognition?
For both of these are indeed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet they are also objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) because they are that which is to be established;
thus, we have a doubt here:
which among these are the means of valid cognition, and which are the objects of valid cognition?
The establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) does not occur through themselves, nor through one another,
nor through the objects of cognition (prameyas), nor indeed without cause. (NagVv 51)
There is no establishment of perception by that very perception; nor of inference by that very inference; nor of comparison by that very comparison; nor of scripture by that very scripture.

Nor [is there establishment] by means of inference, comparison, or scripture for perception; nor by means of perception, comparison, or scripture for inference; nor by means of perception, inference, or scripture for comparison; nor by means of perception, inference, or comparison for scripture. Nor [is there establishment] by means of perceptions, inferences, comparisons, or scriptures other than themselves, each according to its own nature; nor by means of objects of cognition (prameya), whether taken collectively or individually, when they have not grasped their own objects or the objects of others. Nor...
There is no [existence] by chance; rather, there is [existence] through a combination [of causes].
Among these previously mentioned causes—whether twenty, thirty, forty, or thirty-six—that which was stated is as follows:

because objects of cognition (*prameya*) are to be apprehended by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), those objects of cognition do indeed exist, and those valid cognitions also exist, by which valid cognitions those existing objects of cognition are correctly apprehended.
Thus, that is not so.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"Those who understand the states of phenomena consider them to be wholesome phenomena."

They consider the nature of wholesome states to be the same as that of the remaining [unwholesome and neutral] states; this is their application [of the argument]. To this we reply: those who know the states of dharmas say regarding wholesome dharmas: [7] "When wholesome dharmas arise, they do so by depending on a cause. This is what they say. What is the meaning of this? It means that when wholesome dharmas arise, they do not arise without a cause, nor do they arise from an improper cause. What then? They arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "The arising of all phenomena occurs through causes and conditions. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Moreover, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then wholesome dharmas would never arise. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then wholesome dharmas would not arise at all. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various paths and fruits. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the three kinds of roots of goodness, the three kinds of pure actions, the three kinds of right concentration, and the three kinds of right liberation. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various virtues and merits. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four fruits of the ascetic life and the four analytical knowledges. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various fruits and knowledges. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the eighteen elements. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various doctrines and principles. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various meditative concentrations and attainments. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various supreme qualities of a Buddha. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the three trainings, the three gates of liberation, and the three jewels. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various supreme teachings. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four reliances, the four unhindered knowledges, and the four ways of attracting disciples. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various methods of guidance and conversion. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various paths and fruits. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the three kinds of roots of goodness, the three kinds of pure actions, the three kinds of right concentration, and the three kinds of right liberation. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various virtues and merits. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four fruits of the ascetic life and the four analytical knowledges. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various fruits and knowledges. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the eighteen elements. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various doctrines and principles. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various meditative concentrations and attainments. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various supreme qualities of a Buddha. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the three trainings, the three gates of liberation, and the three jewels. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various supreme teachings. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four reliances, the four unhindered knowledges, and the four ways of attracting disciples. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various methods of guidance and conversion. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught these various paths and fruits. Therefore, it is established that wholesome dharmas arise depending on a cause. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dharmas, then the Blessed One would not have taught the three kinds of roots of goodness, the three kinds of pure actions, the three kinds of right concentration, and the three kinds of right liberation. This is because, if there were no cause for the arising of wholesome dh
In this way, the nature of the wholesome itself would have to be expressed through such a distinction.
Those who know the state of phenomena (dharmāvasthāvid) consider the nature of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala*) to be the nature of wholesome persons;
and this must be taught by you through detailed analysis, such as:
"This is that wholesome nature," and "These are those wholesome phenomena."
"This is that wholesome consciousness; this is the very nature of wholesome consciousness"—this is not seen to be the case for all [consciousnesses].
Therefore, what was stated—that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena has been taught—is not tenable.
Furthermore:
if a wholesome intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises in dependence upon those [wholesome factors], then it belongs to the wholesome.
How can the other-nature of phenomena be their very own nature?
And if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wholesome phenomena arises in dependence upon the totality of causes and conditions,
how can that which has arisen from an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) be the intrinsic nature of wholesome phenomena?
The same applies to unwholesome phenomena and so forth.
In that regard, as for what was stated—
that for wholesome and neutral phenomena, a wholesome intrinsic nature is taught,
and likewise for unwholesome phenomena, an unwholesome [nature] and so forth— that is not correct.
Furthermore:
Moreover, if an intrinsic nature were to arise without depending on anything at all, then there would be an abiding of wholesome phenomena, but not of the holy life (brahmacarya). (NagVv 54)
Now, you might think:

"Nothing depending upon anything else gives rise to the wholesome nature of wholesome phenomena; likewise, the unwholesome [nature] of unwholesome phenomena and the indeterminate [nature] of indeterminate phenomena arise [without dependence]."
If this were so, there would be a living of the religious life (abrahmacaryavāsa). Why?
Because if this were so, there would be a rejection of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
From the rejection of dependent origination, there follows a rejection of the vision of dependent origination.
For the vision of dependent origination, being non-existent, cannot arise;
and when there is no vision of dependent origination, there is no vision of the Dharma.
For it has been said:
"Monks, for whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dharma;
in the absence of seeing the Dharma, there is an absence of living the holy life."
Alternatively, by the rejection of dependent origination,
there occurs the rejection of the origin of suffering.
For dependent origination is the origin of suffering.
By the rejection of the origin of suffering, the rejection of suffering occurs;
for if there is no origin, from where will that suffering arise?
And by the rejection of the origin of suffering, there is the rejection of the cessation of suffering;
for if the origin of suffering does not exist, through the abandonment of what will there be cessation?
And if the cessation of suffering does not exist, for the attainment of what will there be a path?
[The path] leading to the cessation of suffering.
Thus, due to the non-existence of the four noble truths, there is a non-existence of the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The fruits of asceticism, such as the vision of the truths and so forth, are attained through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because of the absence of the fruits of the ascetic life, it is a non-living of the holy life.
Furthermore:
Neither non-dharma nor dharma would exist, nor would there be worldly conventional transactions;
moreover, all things would be eternal, because they would be eternal and thus lack a cause.
This being the case, what fault would accrue to you who reject dependent origination?
Neither dharma nor adharma would exist.
Furthermore, worldly conventional transactions would not be possible.
Why? Because all this is dependently originated; if dependent origination did not exist, how could anything come to be?
Moreover, that which possesses intrinsic nature would be non-dependently originated, causeless, and eternal.

What is the reason? For if things were causeless, they would be eternal; in that case, it would follow that one remains in a state of non-celibacy, and there would be a contradiction with your own established doctrine.

Why? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been taught by the Blessed One to be impermanent; if they possessed the permanence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would indeed be eternal.
Furthermore, this same fault applies to unwholesome states, neutral states, and those conducive to liberation and so forth.
Therefore, for you, everything—both the conditioned and the unconditioned—becomes exactly like that.

And this same method that has been explained regarding the wholesome applies likewise to the unwholesome, the indeterminate, and those factors such as the non-leading to liberation; therefore, all of this results in being both conditioned and unconditioned.
For what reason? Because when there is no cause, arising, abiding, and ceasing do not occur;

and when arising, abiding, and ceasing are absent, the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are non-existent. Consequently, everything that is conditioned becomes unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In this regard, that which was stated—that all things are non-empty because wholesome and other such entities exist by way of their own intrinsic nature—is not correct.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"If things had no intrinsic nature, then [the statement] 'there is no intrinsic nature' would likewise..."
Even a name would exist in this way, for indeed there is no name without an object.
One who would say that a truly existent name exists as having intrinsic nature (svabhāva) should be answered by you thus: "We do not say that the name exists as something real. [NagVv 57]
If someone were to say that a name is truly existent, he should be answered by you:
"For which intrinsic nature does this truly existent name belong? Therefore, that intrinsic nature itself must also be truly existent."
For that which is non-existent cannot have an existent name.

Furthermore, we do not claim that the name is existent; for since it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the name is itself without intrinsic nature, and being empty, it is non-existent. Therefore, your statement that "because the name exists, intrinsic nature is existent" is incorrect.
Furthermore:
(Vv 310) Regarding this statement that "name is non-existent," does it refer to something that exists or to something that does not exist?
For whether [the cause] exists or does not exist, in both cases your argument is undermined.
And as for this name "non-existent," does it belong to the existent or to the non-existent?
For if that name belongs to the existent, or if it belongs to the non-existent, in either case the proposition is abandoned.
In that regard, first, if it belongs to the existent:

The proposition that "it is non-existent" is abandoned. For it is not the case that what was non-existent at one time becomes existent at another; thus, the proposition that "it is non-existent" is not the name for that which has become non-existent. Since the name "existent intrinsic nature" (astitva-svabhāva) applies, it follows that the intrinsic nature is indeed existent; therefore, that [proposition] is lost.
Furthermore:
"The emptiness of all things has already been established previously; therefore, that objection does not apply, for this is not a formal proposition. (NagVv 59)
In this context, we have already previously established in detail the emptiness of all entities.
Therein, it was stated even before that name is empty; however, [the opponent] proceeded to speak while assuming that there is no possibility of non-emptiness, thinking:
"If entities were devoid of intrinsic nature, then even this name 'absence of intrinsic nature' would not exist."
Therefore, the objection you raise regarding our lack of a formal thesis does not apply;
for we do not assert that "name" is an existing reality.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"If intrinsic nature exists, yet it does not exist in phenomena, therefore..."
It is logical to teach that for which there is an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from phenomena (dharma); however,
as for the doubt raised— that an intrinsic nature exists while it does not exist in phenomena— this is a doubt that has been rendered groundless.

For we do not negate the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena, nor do we accept the intrinsic nature of any entity whatsoever apart from phenomena. If this is so, does it not follow that there is an objection?
If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, then what other entity, distinct from phenomena, could possibly possess an intrinsic nature?
To suggest that such a thing must be taught would be utterly far-fetched.
Furthermore, as for what you have stated:
"Because this negation applies only to that which exists, as in the case of 'there is no jar in the house'."
"Since this negation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) has been observed by you,
we say in response to this:
if emptiness is the negation of that which exists, then surely this [emptiness] itself is not negated."
For you deny the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) of all things.
If the negation occurs by itself alone,
it negates the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) of things by name;
surely, then, the lack of intrinsic nature of all things has been negated by your own statement.
You negate [emptiness] because of the existence of things;
and since the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all things has been negated,
emptiness itself is negated.
If you negate emptiness, yet that emptiness does not exist,
then your doctrine— that negation applies only to what exists— is surely abandoned.
Now, if you negate emptiness—
the fact that all things lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) being emptiness— and claim that such emptiness does not exist,
then your proposition that "negation applies to what exists, not to what does not exist" is undermined.
(Vv 316) Furthermore: I do not negate anything, nor does there exist anything to be negated.
Therefore, when you say "you negate," you are merely engaging in hyperbole.
Even so, if I were to negate anything at all, then it would indeed be right to say [that my argument is flawed].
But I do not negate anything at all; therefore, there is nothing to be negated.
Consequently, since all things are empty and no object of negation exists, you are here making a truly baseless accusation by saying, "You are negating."
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"If that intrinsic nature does not exist, then what is it that is being negated by you with this statement? For a negation of a non-existent thing is established even without a statement. [12]
To this we reply:

As for what you said—that by my words the statement of the negation of the non-existent is established—here it is made known that speech [itself] is non-existent; it does not refute that [non-existence].

And as for what you say— that even though there is speech, the negation of the non-existent is thereby precluded— [we ask]: in that case, how can it be said that "all things are without intrinsic nature"?
"He performs this speech."
To this we reply: this statement "all things are without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) certainly does not make all things without intrinsic nature;
rather, it makes known that the intrinsic nature of things is non-existent—that is, that they have no intrinsic nature.
In this regard, someone might say: "Devadatta is not in the house," yet [another] says, "Devadatta is in the house."
In that case, someone might reply to him, "He is not there.
That [statement] does not bring about the non-existence of Devadatta;
rather, it merely makes known the absence of Devadatta in the house.
Alternatively, this statement, "entities have no intrinsic nature," does not produce the absence of intrinsic nature in intrinsic natures;
rather, it makes known the non-existence of intrinsic nature within entities.
In this regard, what you have said— that if intrinsic nature does not exist, why does this statement "there is no intrinsic nature" function;
and that even without such a statement, the non-existence of intrinsic nature is established—
is not tenable for you.
As it was said:
"Just as that grasping for water by fools in a mirage."
In this way, there would be a false apprehension on your part, for that which is non-existent is established [as such].
As for what you said regarding the mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*), we reply:
concerning the example of the mirage, the extensive discussion you have further mentioned—
In this regard as well, hear the definitive conclusion as to how that illustration is logically consistent.
As for the great discussion you have raised regarding the analogy of the mirage, listen to the conclusion reached therein: that very analogy is indeed appropriate.
If that entity were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would not be something arisen dependently (*pratītyasamudbhūta*).
And that apprehension which arises dependently—is it not indeed emptiness itself?
And if that apprehension of water in a mirage were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
it would not be dependently originated;
for it arises in dependence upon the mirage, in dependence upon a distorted perception, and in dependence upon improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*).
Therefore, it has arisen dependently; and because it has arisen dependently, it is indeed empty of intrinsic nature, just as was stated previously. (Vv 322)
Furthermore:
And if the grasping were to exist by way of intrinsic nature, who could turn that grasping back?
This same rule applies to the remaining [categories] as well; therefore, this is not a valid objection.
And if the apprehension of water in a mirage were due to its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
who could ever turn it back?
For an intrinsic nature cannot be overturned.
Just as heat is the nature of fire, fluidity that of water, and non-obstruction that of space,
yet their cessation is observed;
therefore, grasping has emptiness as its intrinsic nature.
And since this is so, this same sequence should be understood to apply to the remaining five categories of objects of apprehension as well.
In that regard, your claim that "all things are non-empty" is not tenable.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"And your reason is not established because of [all things'] lack of intrinsic nature; for from where could your reason come?"
Furthermore, the establishment of this object of yours as being without a cause is not tenable. [l7]
To this we reply:
by this, the absence of a reason has already been refuted previously, because it is equal [to the case at hand],
as was stated earlier regarding the exclusion of the example of a mirage.
By this very same discussion already mentioned, the absence of a reason (*hetvabhāva*) should also be understood.
For the very same argument that was stated regarding the previous reason—concerning the refutation of the group of six (*ṣaṭka*)—must also be applied here.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"If the negation comes first and the object to be negated later, it is untenable;
and it is also untenable if they come later, or if they are simultaneous, because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) does not exist. [20]
To this we reply: that which was previously stated regarding the refutation of the reason in the three times applies here as well, because of its equality;
and a counter-reason for the three times is established through the state of emptiness and so forth.
This very reason, which expresses a negation regarding the three times, has already been answered by the opponent.
Why? Because it is equal to the point to be proven (*sādhyasamatvāt*).
For just as a negation is not tenable in the three times, so too is the negation of that negation.
Therefore, your notion that a negation is established when there is neither a negation nor an object to be negated is incorrect.

For this very reason, this logical reason—which expresses a negation of the three times—is obtained by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyatāvādins*) because it negates the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all things; it is not yours.
Alternatively, how can this have been answered?
"I do not negate anything, nor does there exist anything to be negated; therefore, this is a groundless reproach made by you when you say, 'You negate.'"
(Vv 328) Now, if you think that [causality] exists in all three times— namely, that a cause is observed as being either prior in time, posterior in time,
or simultaneous in time.
How is it prior in time?
As when, according to your own statement, the father is posterior in time to the son;
as when the disciple is simultaneous in time with the teacher; and as when the lamp is [simultaneous] with its illumination.
To this we reply:
this is not at all tenable, for within these three [positions] the aforementioned fault persists.
Moreover, if this is indeed the case,
you are admitting the existence of negation,
and your original thesis is thereby abandoned.
"Even fuel becomes fire by its own nature.
(Vv 330) "For whom this emptiness is possible, for him all things are possible."
For whom emptiness does not prevail, what does not prevail? For whom emptiness prevails, nothing does not prevail.
For one for whom this emptiness is possible, all aims—both mundane and supramundane—are possible.
Why is that?
For it is for one for whom emptiness is possible that dependent origination is possible.
For whom dependent origination is possible, for them the four noble truths are possible;
for whom the four noble truths are [possible],
for them there arise the fruits of the path and the attainment of all distinctions.
For one in whom all specific realizations arise,
for that person the Three Jewels— the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha— arise.
For one in whom dependent origination arises, for that person the Dharma, the cause of the Dharma, and the fruit of the Dharma arise.
For such a person, unrighteousness, the cause of unrighteousness, and the fruit of unrighteousness arise;
for such a person, affliction, the origin of affliction, and the bases of affliction arise.
For one in whom all this previously mentioned exists, there is the establishment of good and bad destinies, and the going to a good or bad destiny.
The path leading to happy and miserable destinies,

the transcendence of going to happy and miserable destinies, the means for transcending happy and miserable destinies, and all worldly conventions must be realized by oneself. In this manner, something can be taught through words.
And there is this [verse] here:
"He who [sees] emptiness, dependent origination, and the middle way..."
He spoke of many meanings: "I bow to that peerless one, indeed to the Buddha."
This work is by the venerable teacher Nāgārjuna; [it consists of] one hundred and forty-five verses in total.
This was written by Śrī Dharmakīrti for the sake of all sentient beings, just as it was obtained.
